case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with Gorlin syndrome and a 10-year history of daily vismodegib therapy (150 mg) for locally advanced and metastatic basal cell carcinoma presented with worsening watery diarrhea. Two years after starting vismodegib, he developed loose stools 2–3 times daily (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 1), with no interruptions in therapy. A colonoscopy after 5 years of vismodegib was unremarkable; at 9 years it showed mildly granular mucosa with loss of vascular pattern in the ascending and transverse colon, and random biopsies exhibited chronic inactive colitis without erosions, ulcers, granulomas, metaplasia, or dysplasia.

At 10 years of therapy, he had grade 2 diarrhea only partially responsive to loperamide (up to 5 doses daily). He also had alopecia, dysgeusia, and muscle spasms, although these did not correlate with diarrheal episodes. He denied abdominal pain, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel with electrolytes, thyroid-stimulating hormone, tissue transglutaminase antibody, immunoglobulin A, and a multiplex stool PCR panel for bacterial and viral pathogens, were normal or negative.

A repeat colonoscopy revealed diffuse mild ileal edema and granularity with punctate erosions and exudate, as well as colonic edema, granularity, and loss of vascular pattern. Ileal biopsies showed mild villous blunting, active ileitis, chronic lamina propria inflammation, and epithelial apoptosis. Biopsies from the right colon, left colon, and rectum demonstrated crypt architectural distortion, mixed inflammation, epithelial apoptosis, and a crypt abscess. Immunostains for cytomegalovirus were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Broad differential diagnosis including infection, ischemia, graft-versus-host disease, IBD, and drug effects — “The nonspecific histologic findings in this case yield a broad differential diagnosis of infectious causes (including viral infections), ischemia, graft-versus-host disease, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and medication/drug effects.” 2. Epithelial apoptosis suggests a medication-related etiology (also seen in graft-versus-host disease and viral infections) — “the presence of epithelial apoptosis raises the likelihood of a medication-related etiology because epithelial apoptosis is characteristically associated with medication effects, graft-versus-host disease, and viral infections.” 3. Infectious etiologies excluded by negative molecular and immunohistochemical studies — “the result of polymerase chain reaction–based testing for infectious etiologies (including bacterial and viral entities) was negative. A cytomegalovirus stain performed on the tissue was also negative.” 4. IBD considered but less likely given absence of pronounced active inflammation and presence of epithelial apoptosis — “IBD typically presents with a more pronounced active inflammatory infiltrate and lack of epithelial apoptosis.” 5. Medication effect deemed most likely based on clinicopathologic correlation — “These findings led us to conclude that a medication/drug effect was the most likely etiology.”

selection.screen_reason: Chronic watery diarrhea during long-term vismodegib with negative infectious and celiac workup and apoptotic colitis on biopsy points to a drug effect.
selection.second_look_note: Watery diarrhea emerging during ten years of vismodegib with a negative infectious and celiac workup and apoptotic ileocolitis; the drug history is the key clue.
